narration_use: reference only when drafting; required units must be derivable from the public B2 inputs (table + intent)
file_naming: one G1 per input contract; B1/B3/B4/B5 need separate drafts
intent: To demonstrate that telephone survey results for partisan identification are consistent with those from established federal surveys like the General Social Survey.

units.meaning: The clip compares two survey sources—Pew Research Center and General Social Survey—on partisan identification, with separate Democratic and Republican entities.

basis.note: Example value from the Pew Democratic series
Example value from the GSS Democratic series
Example value from the Pew Republican series
Example value from the GSS Republican series

accepted_routes: The video compares Pew Research Center telephone surveys with the General Social Survey for Democratic and Republican identification.
Two sources (Pew and GSS) are shown for each party (Democratic and Republican).
Partisan identification is broken out by survey source: Pew vs GSS, Democrats vs Republicans.
units.visual_evidence_rule: Labels or legend identify Pew Research Center and General Social Survey, and both Democratic and Republican entities are present.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about 'telephone surveys' and 'federal surveys'
units.reviewer_question: Must the video name both source series and both partisan groups, or can it show only the comparison numerically?

units.meaning: At the aligned 2010 comparison, Pew and GSS give very similar Democratic identification values: Pew 35.11% vs GSS 33.11%, a gap of about 2 percentage points.

basis.note: Pew Democratic identification at aligned 2010 tick
GSS Democratic identification at aligned 2010 tick

accepted_routes: At 2010, Pew puts Democratic identification at 35.11% and GSS at 33.11%, a gap of about 2 points.
Democratic identification is roughly 35% in Pew and 33% in GSS in 2010.
Both sources give nearly the same Democratic share in 2010 (about 33–35%).
units.visual_evidence_rule: The Democratic Pew and GSS series are shown at the same 2010 time point with close values (about 35.11% vs 33.11%).
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about 'very similar numbers' or 'Democrats'
units.reviewer_question: Is the 2010 Democratic cross-source closeness required, or can the video convey consistency only at a general level?

units.meaning: At the aligned 2010 comparison, Pew and GSS give very similar Republican identification values: Pew 24.13% vs GSS 21.63%, a gap of about 2.5 percentage points.

basis.note: Pew Republican identification at aligned 2010 tick
GSS Republican identification at aligned 2010 tick

accepted_routes: At 2010, Pew puts Republican identification at 24.13% and GSS at 21.63%, a gap of about 2.5 points.
Republican identification is roughly 24% in Pew and 22% in GSS in 2010.
Both sources give similar Republican shares in 2010 (low 20s).
units.visual_evidence_rule: The Republican Pew and GSS series are shown at the same 2010 time point with close values (about 24.13% vs 21.63%).
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about 'very similar numbers' or 'Republicans'
units.reviewer_question: Is the 2010 Republican cross-source closeness required, or is it enough to show overall similarity?

units.meaning: For Republican identification, both Pew and GSS show a downward trend from 1990 to 2010, with GSS also ending at 21.24% in 2016.
units.computation: Pew decline: 30.12 - 24.13 = 5.99 percentage points; GSS decline: 32.12 - 21.63 = 10.49 percentage points (GSS 1990 to 2016: 32.12 - 21.24 = 10.88)
accepted_routes: Republican identification falls in both surveys: Pew 30.12% in 1990 to 24.13% in 2010; GSS 32.12% in 1990 to 21.63% in 2010, and 21.24% in 2016.
Both Pew and GSS trend downward for Republicans, though the GSS drop is steeper.
From 1990 onward, both sources show a decline in Republican identification.
units.visual_evidence_rule: Republican Pew and GSS series are shown sloping downward from 1990 to later years (2010/2016).
units.temporal_anchor: the time-series portion of the clip, if the animation shows multiple years
units.reviewer_question: Is the shared downward Republican trend required, or optional context?

units.meaning: At the aligned 2010 comparison, both sources show Democratic identification exceeding Republican identification by about 11 percentage points.
units.computation: Pew: 35.11 - 24.13 = 10.98 percentage points; GSS: 33.11 - 21.63 = 11.48 percentage points
accepted_routes: At 2010, both sources show Democratic identification about 11 percentage points higher than Republican identification.
Pew: Democrats 35.11% vs Republicans 24.13%; GSS: Democrats 33.11% vs Republicans 21.63%.
Democrats lead Republicans in both survey sources at 2010.
units.visual_evidence_rule: At 2010, Democratic series values are visibly above Republican series values for both Pew and GSS.
units.temporal_anchor: the narration clause about 'what share of Americans identify as Republicans versus Democrats'
units.reviewer_question: Is the Democratic-over-Republican comparison at the aligned 2010 point required?

optional_valid: Democratic series stability/range: Pew Democratic values run from 28.13% to 38.11%; GSS Democratic values run from 30.92% to 34.91%, both generally in the low 30s.
1990 Republican cross-source gap: Pew 30.12% vs GSS 32.12%, difference 2.0 percentage points.
unsupported_to_avoid: Claiming the telephone survey is accurate or representative because it matches GSS (causal claim).
Saying the two sources are identical or that every year matches exactly.
Summing Democratic and Republican shares to 100% or referring to Independents, since the table only has Democratic and Republican percentages.
Extrapolating beyond 2016 or asserting a national total.
Using chart positions, colors, axis ticks, or line styles as semantic content.
notes: The core G1 content is cross-source consistency at aligned 2010 and the Democratic-over-Republican ordering. Trend and the 1990 Republican comparison are valid but optional relative to the narration.
weight_mode_note: every unit gets 1/n so coverage is a plain share; weight_template is kept for per-type analysis only
